\chapter{In the House}
\label{ch:sa-house}
\hlchaptermodality{35}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name five things in a house in Sanskrit, and say which one of them came into the language from Persian.}

Complete SA-C35-bed and demonstrate the chapter promise.

\section[dugdham]{\sk{दुग्धम्} (dugdham) — milk}

\label{lesson:SA-C35-milk}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{dehaḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{दुग्धम्}}
\textbf{\sk{दुग्धम्}} (\emph{dugdham}) — \textquotedblleft{}milk\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit has two words for milk. You met \emph{kṣīram} early on; \textbf{\sk{दुग्धम्}} is the other one, and it is the one the modern languages kept.

It comes from \emph{duh}, \textquotedblleft{}to milk\textquotedblright{}, so \textbf{\sk{दुग्धम्}} is \textquotedblleft{}the milked thing\textquotedblright{} — the action first, the drink second. Hindi and Gujarati say \emph{dūdh}, Punjabi \emph{duddh}, and you can hear the whole word still inside them. Neuter \textbf{-\sk{अम्}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The second word for milk, and the one you would be handed today.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{dugdham}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{dehaḥ}, then \emph{dugdham}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{दुग्धम्} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}milk\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[madhu]{\sk{मधु} (madhu) — honey}

\label{lesson:SA-C35-honey}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{dugdham} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{मधु}}
\textbf{\sk{मधु}} (\emph{madhu}) — \textquotedblleft{}honey\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{मधु}} is honey, and sweetness in general.

Almost nothing in this book has cousins this far-flung. English \emph{mead} is the same word; Greek \emph{methu} is wine, and \emph{amethyst} — \emph{a-methustos}, \textquotedblleft{}not drunk\textquotedblright{} — is the stone that was thought to keep you sober; Lithuanian \emph{medus} and Old Irish \emph{mid} are honey and mead again. Even Chinese \emph{mì}, \textquotedblleft{}honey\textquotedblright{}, was borrowed from an early Indo-European neighbour. Ends in short \emph{-u}, like \textbf{\sk{साधु}} and \textbf{\sk{दारु}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Honey, and a word that reached from Ireland to China.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{madhu}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{dugdham}, then \emph{madhu}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{मधु} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}honey\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[lavaṇam]{\sk{लवणम्} (lavaṇam) — salt}

\label{lesson:SA-C35-salt}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{madhu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{लवणम्}}
\textbf{\sk{लवणम्}} (\emph{lavaṇam}) — \textquotedblleft{}salt\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{लवणम्}} is salt, and salty as a taste.

Here Sanskrit went its own way: Latin \emph{sal} and English \emph{salt} come from a different old word altogether, and \textbf{\sk{लवणम्}} has no cousin among them. It stayed at home instead — \emph{lavaṇa} still names the salty one among the six tastes of Indian cooking, while everyday Hindi took \emph{namak} from Persian for the thing in the jar. Neuter \textbf{-\sk{अम्}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Salt, and a word with no European relatives at all.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{lavaṇam}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{madhu}, then \emph{lavaṇam}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{लवणम्} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}salt\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pustakam]{\sk{पुस्तकम्} (pustakam) — a book}

\label{lesson:SA-C35-book}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{lavaṇam} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{पुस्तकम्}}
\textbf{\sk{पुस्तकम्}} (\emph{pustakam}) — \textquotedblleft{}a book\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{पुस्तकम्}} is a traveller. It came into Sanskrit from Persian \emph{post}, \textquotedblleft{}hide, skin\textquotedblright{} — what a book was written on before paper — and then India handed it back out again.

Hindi \emph{pustak}, Bengali \emph{pustak}, Kannada \emph{pustaka}, Telugu \emph{pustakam} and Tamil \emph{puttakam} are all this word. Most of what you have learned here was inherited; this one was borrowed, and you can tell, because its relatives live outside the language rather than inside it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A book, and the one borrowed word in the chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pustakam}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{lavaṇam}, then \emph{pustakam}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{पुस्तकम्} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a book\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[śayyā]{\sk{शय्या} (śayyā) — a bed}

\label{lesson:SA-C35-bed}



\begin{quote}
Before the last word of the chapter: what did \emph{pustakam} mean, and what did \emph{dugdham} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{शय्या}}
\textbf{\sk{शय्या}} (\emph{śayyā}) — \textquotedblleft{}a bed\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{शय्या}} comes from \emph{śī}, \textquotedblleft{}to lie down\textquotedblright{}, so a bed is simply the lying-down place.

Its cousins settle rather than sleep: Greek \emph{keitai}, \textquotedblleft{}he lies\textquotedblright{}; Latin \emph{cīvis}, a citizen — one who lies down in a place instead of moving on — behind \emph{city}, \emph{civil} and \emph{civilian}; and English \emph{home}, and \emph{hide}, once a measure of land a single family could settle. A bed and a city turn out to be one idea at two sizes. Ends in \textbf{-\sk{आ}}, like \textbf{\sk{लता}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five things in a house, and a bed with a city inside it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{śayyā}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then say which one came in from Persian
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{शय्या} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a bed\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
